'''Jordan Peterson''' is a Canadian clinical psychologist and author who became one of the most widely-followed — and most polarizing — public intellectuals of the late 2010s. He appears in [[Media and Personalities]] as a thinker whose framework (psychology of meaning, myth, and responsibility) drives a large share of the surrounding discourse.

== Who he is ==

A clinical psychologist and former University of Toronto professor, Peterson spent decades on the psychology of belief and personality before his first book, '''''Maps of Meaning''''' (1999), laid out his lifelong project: reading myth, religion, and story as encoded maps of how humans find meaning and order chaos. He came to mass attention in 2016 over his opposition to Canada's Bill C-16 and compelled-speech concerns, and his second book, '''''12 Rules for Life''''', became a global bestseller.

== What he argues ==

His throughlines: '''meaning over happiness''' (a life is sustained by responsibility and a worthy burden, not by comfort); '''order and chaos''' as the fundamental psychological categories, dramatized through myth and the hero's journey; the '''Jungian / archetypal''' reading of religious stories as true "in a psychological sense"; and individual responsibility as the ground of a good life ("clean your room" before you remake the world). His long '''Biblical lecture series''' extended this into a line-by-line psychological reading of Genesis and beyond.

== The strong case ==

At his best he is a serious synthesizer of clinical psychology, mythology, and moral philosophy, and an unusually effective one — he reached millions of (often young, often adrift) people with a message of responsibility, competence, and meaning that genuinely helped many of them. His archetypal readings of scripture are a real contribution to how a secular audience can take religious texts seriously.

== The weak case ==

He is also prone to grandiosity, to a verbose and sometimes evasive style, and to extending psychological authority into political, climate, and policy claims where his expertise runs out and the certainty does not. His framings can flatten complex social questions, and his later public career has been as much culture-war lightning rod as scholarship. Read the psychology-of-meaning core as the strong material, and treat the broad political pronouncements as contested opinion.
